title: Condition-Based vs Preventive Maintenance: Which to Choose (With a 12-Month Cost Example)
summary: Condition-based vs preventive maintenance compared on trigger, labor and cost, with a 12-month worked example on one asset class.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- Preventive maintenance fits wear that follows the calendar or run hours, such as lubrication and filter changes.
- Condition-based maintenance fits critical rotating assets whose failures arrive at random, where a fixed interval misses the fault or replaces a healthy part.
- The worked example below shows 12 pump sets costing $49,150 less per year on condition-based work than on PM intervals before monitoring costs.


Choose preventive maintenance for wear that tracks time or usage, and condition-based maintenance for critical assets whose failures don't follow a schedule. Many plants run both: the calendar keeps the lubrication and compliance tasks, and sensor data decides when the bearings, couplings and seals on critical machines get work.


The 12-month cost model below runs on a fleet of 12 pump and motor sets with the math on the page, so you can rerun it with your own numbers. Predictive maintenance is covered alongside both in this[three-way comparison of preventive, predictive and condition-based maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/blog/preventive-vs-predictive-vs-condition-based-maintenance) .


## What is the difference between condition-based and preventive maintenance?


[Preventive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/preventive-maintenance) triggers work on a time or usage interval, such as a 90-day or 2,000-run-hour interval, whatever the machine's condition. Condition-based maintenance triggers work when a measured signal, such as vibration, temperature or ultrasound, shows a developing fault.


The practical difference shows up in the labor plan. A PM calendar is easy to staff because the work is known months ahead, but it spends hours on machines that are fine. Condition-based work is scheduled from the data, so the crew opens a machine when it has a reason to.


Learn more about[condition-based maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/condition-based-maintenance) .


Factor Preventive maintenance Condition-based maintenance


What triggers the work A date, run hours or a cycle count A measured change in vibration, temperature, ultrasound or another condition signal


Data needed Asset list, intervals, OEM recommendations and task history A baseline for each machine plus continuous or periodic readings


Labor pattern Fixed and easy to staff, including tasks on machines that are fine Set by findings, with fewer routine tasks and repairs booked ahead


Failure modes it handles well Wear tied to age or use: lubricant breakdown, filter loading, belt stretch, worn wear parts Faults that start at random: bearing defects, misalignment, imbalance, looseness, lubrication starvation


What it misses Faults that start and progress between two visits Failure modes the chosen signals can't see, and machines with no sensor


Cost profile Low setup cost, steady labor and parts spend, some parts replaced early A monitoring cost per asset, less routine labor, fewer emergency repairs


Typical assets Redundant or low-criticality equipment, HVAC filters, conveyors with spares in stores, mandated safety checks Critical pumps, motors, fans, gearboxes and compressors where a stop halts production


## When does preventive maintenance still make sense?


Preventive maintenance still makes sense when a failure mode tracks time or use closely, when a regulation or insurer requires the task on a fixed date, or when the asset is cheap and backed by a spare. In those cases the interval lands close to the right moment and costs little to run.


- Age and usage wear. Belts, filters, wear plates and motor brushes degrade at a fairly steady rate, so an interval set on run hours lands near the end of their useful life.
- **Lubrication and consumables.** Grease points, oil changes and filter swaps are short tasks, and a route bundles dozens of them into one walk.
- **Regulatory and safety tasks.** Pressure vessel inspections, fire pump tests and lockout device checks stay on the calendar whatever a sensor reads.
- **Low-cost, redundant assets.** A small exhaust fan with a spare in stores costs less to run on a simple interval, or even to failure, than to instrument.


The weak spot is the stretch between two visits. A bearing defect can start the week after a quarterly inspection and reach failure before the next one, while the PM record still shows the task as done. Teams chasing[preventive maintenance compliance](https://tractian.com/en/blog/preventive-maintenance-compliance-strategies) targets can hit them and still miss these faults.


Interval work also opens machines that are healthy. Each teardown and reassembly is a chance for a maintenance-induced failure, such as a misaligned coupling, a contaminated bearing or an over-greased housing.


## When does condition-based maintenance pay off?


Condition-based maintenance pays off where a failure is expensive and arrives without a predictable date: bottleneck machines, equipment with long spare-part lead times, and rotating assets whose bearing and alignment faults start at random. On those assets, a reading that shows the fault early is worth more than a shorter interval.


The[P-F interval](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/p-f-curve-potential-failure-curve) explains why. It is the time between the point a fault becomes detectable (P) and functional failure (F). If readings arrive often enough to land inside that window, the team sees the fault with time to order parts and plan the repair.


- **Bottleneck assets.** One process pump or mixer drive whose stop idles the whole line.
- **Long lead-time parts.** Large motors, custom gearboxes and specialty seals that take weeks or months to source.
- **High downtime cost.** Lines where an hour of lost production costs more than the repair itself.
- **Random failure patterns.** Assets whose failure history shows no clear age pattern, so a tighter interval adds labor without adding protection.


A[criticality analysis](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/criticality-analysis) ranks which assets pass these tests first.


### The run-to-failure cascade on one motor


Take an example with illustrative figures. A $50 bearing starts to spall on the drive end of a pump motor, and nobody opens the machine until the next scheduled visit.


Left running, the bearing overheats and the damage spreads to the $5,000 shaft. Run it longer and the heat and rub burn out the $50,000 motor, often on a night shift with no spare in stores.


Caught inside the P-F window, the same fault is a planned bearing change during a scheduled stop. That gap between a $50 part and a $50,000 replacement is the logic behind the 12-month model below.


## What does each approach cost over 12 months on one asset class?


In the example model below, a fleet of 12 critical pump and motor sets costs $80,775 a year on a preventive schedule and $31,625 on condition-based work, before the cost of monitoring. Most of the $49,150 gap comes from two fewer unplanned failures, and the inputs are example numbers you can swap for your own.


### The assumptions


- 12 critical centrifugal pump and motor sets, each running about 8,000 hours a year.
- Loaded labor rate of $75 an hour on shift and $112.50 an hour on overtime.
- $350 in bearings, seals and lubricant for one planned bearing change, which takes 6 hours.
- One unplanned failure costs 10 hours of overtime labor, $3,000 in parts including secondary damage, and 8 hours of lost production.
- Lost production is valued at $2,000 per hour of downtime.
- Planned work in both plans happens during scheduled stops, so it carries no lost-production cost.


These figures are examples for illustration, not Tractian data and not a forecast for your plant.


### The preventive maintenance year


The PM plan inspects each set quarterly at 3 hours per visit and swaps the bearings once a year whether they need it or not. In this example, 3 faults still start and progress between visits and end in unplanned failures.


- Inspections: 48 visits x 3 h = 144 h.
- Annual bearing swaps: 12 x 6 h = 72 h, plus 12 x $350 = $4,200 in parts.
- Planned labor: 216 h x $75 = $16,200.
- Unplanned failures: 3 x (10 h x $112.50 + $3,000 + 8 h x $2,000) = 3 x $20,125 = $60,375.
- Total: $16,200 + $4,200 + $60,375 = $80,775.


### The condition-based year


The condition-based plan keeps a 1-hour quarterly walk-down and lubrication task on each set and adds 1 hour a week for a planner or technician to review alerts across the fleet. Bearings change when the data shows a developing defect, which happens on 5 of the 12 sets in this example.


One failure still gets through, for instance a fault that develops faster than the readings pick it up.


- Calendar tasks: 48 x 1 h = 48 h.
- Alert review: 52 x 1 h = 52 h.
- Condition-triggered bearing changes: 5 x 6 h = 30 h, plus 5 x $350 = $1,750 in parts.
- Planned labor: 130 h x $75 = $9,750.
- Unplanned failure: 1 x $20,125 = $20,125.
- Total before monitoring: $9,750 + $1,750 + $20,125 = $31,625.

Alert review hours 0 h 52 h 52 weeks x 1 h


Planned bearing changes 12 (72 h) 5 (30 h) Changes x 6 h

To rerun the model, use: annual cost = (calendar hours + review hours + planned repair hours) x shift rate + planned parts + unplanned failures x (emergency hours x overtime rate + emergency parts + downtime hours x lost production per hour).


The result swings most on the failure count. If 2 failures get through under condition-based work instead of 1, that year costs $51,750 and the gap narrows to $29,025.


Subtract the monitoring quote from the gap to get the net saving. Spread across 12 sets, the $49,150 gap leaves about $4,096 per asset per year before the condition-based plan stops paying back in this example.


Learn more about[calculating condition-based maintenance ROI](https://tractian.com/en/blog/how-to-calculate-the-roi-of-condition-based-maintenance) .


### What the difference means for overtime and MTBF


Overtime drops from 30 emergency hours to 10, which for the crew means two fewer night or weekend callouts in the year. Fleet[mean time between failures (MTBF)](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/mean-time-between-failure) rises from 32,000 to 96,000 hours: 96,000 run hours across the fleet divided by 3 failures, then by 1.


Planned work also grows as a share of maintenance hours, from 216 of 246 hours (88%) in the PM year to 130 of 140 (93%) in the condition-based year. Each condition-triggered repair leaves a record of the asset, the alert, the fault found and the failure avoided, which is the evidence a plant manager asks for before approving the next asset class.


## How do you move a PM plan to condition-based maintenance without losing coverage?


Switch one asset class at a time and keep its PM tasks in place until the condition data has shown it can replace them. The steps below keep coverage continuous while the plan changes.


1. Rank assets by criticality. Score each one on production impact, safety, repair cost and spare-part lead time.
2. **Pick the first asset class.** Start with a group of similar critical machines, such as process pumps or fan motors, so baselines and alerts are comparable.
3. **Keep the age-based tasks.** Fixed-volume lubrication, filter changes and mandated inspections stay on the calendar for now.
4. **Set baselines.** Let the sensors record each machine under normal load before acting on its alerts.
5. **Retire intervals as the data proves them.** When an asset's readings stay stable through a full PM cycle, stretch or drop that inspection and note why.
6. **Track the planned vs unplanned maintenance ratio and MTBF.** Compare them each month against the year before the switch.
7. **Report prevented failures.** Give leadership each catch with the asset, the fault, the repair and the cost avoided.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is condition-based maintenance cheaper than preventive maintenance?


It can be, on critical assets whose failures start at random, because it cuts emergency repairs and routine tasks on machines that are running fine. In the example model in this post, the gap is $49,150 a year across 12 pump sets before the cost of monitoring. On cheap, redundant equipment, a simple preventive interval can cost less than instrumenting it.


### Can you run preventive and condition-based maintenance together?


Yes, and the mix is common. Calendar tasks stay for lubrication, consumables and mandated inspections, while sensor data decides when to open the critical rotating machines. Tractian sends its alerts into the existing CMMS, so both kinds of work land in one backlog.


### Which assets should stay on a preventive schedule?


Keep assets whose wear follows time or usage closely, assets with mandated inspection dates, and low-cost equipment with a spare on the shelf. Filters, belts, grease points, fire pump tests and small redundant fans are typical examples.


### How do you set condition-based maintenance thresholds?


Record a baseline of each machine running under normal load, then alert on a change from that baseline instead of one fixed number for the whole fleet. General vibration severity charts give a starting point, and the asset's own trend refines it over time. Tractian learns how each machine runs under normal conditions and flags deviations from that behavior.


### How long does it take to switch an asset class to condition-based maintenance?


The hardware side is quick: Tractian sensors go on in a single day, and the platform reaches full visibility within the first 14 days as it learns each machine. Retiring the old PM intervals takes longer. Plan on at least one full PM cycle of stable readings per asset before stretching or dropping an inspection.
